summary: A white paper on security worries about some IPng candidates, saying IPng need not improve on IPv4 but must not make security worse. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A warning that the new Internet should not be less safe than the old one.

subtitle: A security analyst's checklist: IPng must not make networks harder to protect.

tldr.problem: Several IPng candidates have features that could weaken network security if left unchecked.
tldr.mechanism: A careful analysis of firewall requirements, encryption and authentication, source routing, and accounting identifies areas where IPng design choices could hinder or help defense.
tldr.outcome: IPng need not improve on IPv4 security, but it must not make networks less defensible or weaken the existing security infrastructure.

today: RFC 1675 is Informational from August 1994. IPv6 eventually addressed many of these concerns through IPsec integration and careful address design, though source routing support was eventually removed from IPv6, partly for security reasons consistent with Bellovin's analysis.

sections.title: Security in IPng Design
sections.content:
RFC 1675 is a white paper from Steven Bellovin at AT&T Bell Laboratories on security concerns for IPng candidates. Bellovin emphasizes that while IPng need not improve on IPv4 security, it is mandatory that it not make things worse. His analysis identifies areas where IPng design choices could create new vulnerabilities or eliminate existing defensive mechanisms.

The RFC addresses firewalls, encryption and authentication, source routing, address-based authentication, and accounting—areas where the network architecture affects whether sites can defend themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Bellovin says IPng design choices will make some security problems worse or easier to fix; designers must be aware of the tradeoffs.

sections.title: Firewalls and Filtering
sections.content:
Firewalls are a critical defensive tool, compensating for buggy software and poor system administration. IPng must not make firewalls harder to deploy. Firewalls require a hierarchical address space (good for routing scalability too), access to both source and destination addresses, and access to transport-layer headers (TCP/UDP ports and TCP ACK bits for distinguishing incoming from outgoing calls).

One transition plan uses network-level packet translators. Organizations with firewalls must be able to deploy their own translators for their internal networks; they cannot rely on centralized translators. These translators must be simple, portable, and inexpensive—but not usable for connection-laundering, as that would make attack tracing harder.
sections.plainLanguage: Firewalls need to see addresses and port numbers clearly. They need to be simple enough for any organization to build. They should not let attackers hide their tracks.

sections.title: Encryption and Authentication Trade-offs
sections.content:
IP-level encryption and cryptographic authentication are increasingly important and must continue to be possible. Encryption can be done at different granularities (host-to-host, host-to-gateway, gateway-to-gateway) and IPng must not rule out any. Encapsulation and tunneling can obscure source addresses, creating constraints on network topology that users should understand.

Dual-stack approaches (running both stacks on the same host) imply multiple addresses per host. Encryption and access control infrastructure must know about all addresses for a host and prevent bypassing authentication by requesting a different stack's address.

Source routing, a proposed feature for some IPng candidates, breaks address-based authentication (the most common form today). If source routing is used, cryptographic authentication must be deployed first and widely.
sections.plainLanguage: Users should be able to encrypt traffic. Dual-stack networks need careful security planning. Source routing breaks simple authentication, so it needs real cryptography if adopted.

sections.title: Accounting and Non-intrusive Authentication
sections.content:
Usage-sensitive accounting and quality-of-service billing require definitive knowledge of source and destination addresses. IPng should support a non-intrusive packet authentication mechanism: one that imposes little load on intermediate routers that do not need authentication, can be removed by border gateways if desired, and is ignorable by systems to which it does not apply.

Bellovin argues that security requirements around accounting are manageable if designed carefully, but careless design could create new attack surfaces or undermine existing defenses.
sections.plainLanguage: Billing systems need to trust what packets say about who sent them, but that checking should not slow down routers or create new ways to attack the network.

references.text: Gross, P. (ed.), "Internet Next Generation Architecture", RFC 1550, December 1993.
